content: Plague is an uncommon infectious disease caused by bacteria that can affect both humans and animals. Humans can contract plague through several routes: being bitten by fleas infected with the bacteria, handling an infected animal, or inhaling infectious respiratory droplets from an infected person or animal. The symptoms of plague vary depending on the mode of exposure to the bacteria. Plague manifests in different clinical forms, with the most common types in humans being bubonic plague, septicemic plague, and pneumonic plague. Bubonic plague is typically transmitted through bites from infected fleas or by handling infected animals. Symptoms include fever, headache, chills, and the development of painful, swollen, and tender lymph nodes, known as buboes. Septicemic plague can also result from flea bites or contact with infected animals. Symptoms include fever, chills, weakness, abdominal pain, and, in some cases, bleeding into the skin and other organs. The skin and other tissues, particularly on the fingers, toes, and nose, may turn black and necrotic. Pneumonic plague occurs when a person inhales infectious respiratory droplets from an infected individual or animal. It can also develop as a complication of untreated bubonic or septicemic plague. Symptoms include fever, weakness, shortness of breath, chest pain, and a cough that produces bloody or watery mucus. Plague is found in specific regions, including parts of Africa, Central Asia, the Indian subcontinent, northern South America, and the southwestern United States. Urban outbreaks have been reported in Madagascar. While the risk to travelers is generally low, activities such as camping, hunting, hiking, or working outdoors in plague-endemic areas can increase the likelihood of exposure. There is currently no vaccine available in the United States to prevent plague. However, travelers can take several precautions to reduce their risk: 1. Use EPA-registered insect repellents containing active ingredients such as picaridin, oil of lemon eucalyptus (OLE), or para-menthane-diol (PMD). These repellents are safe and effective when used as directed, even for pregnant and breastfeeding women. 2. Treat clothing and gear with 0.5% permethrin or purchase pre-treated items. Permethrin is an insecticide that kills or repels insects. Follow product instructions carefully and avoid applying permethrin directly to the skin. 3. Avoid contact with sick or dead animals, as infected fleas can jump from these animals onto humans. Handling tissues or body fluids of infected animals, such as during hunting or skinning, can also lead to infection. If handling such animals is unavoidable, wear gloves, long sleeves, and other protective clothing to minimize exposure. Additional measures for those living in or visiting plague-endemic areas include: Storing food, including pet food, in rodent-proof containers. Keeping rodents out of living spaces and ensuring homes are rodent-proof. Protecting pets from fleas and consulting a veterinarian for advice. Avoiding allowing free-roaming pets in plague-endemic areas to sleep on your bed. Plague is a severe illness but is treatable with commonly available antibiotics. Early medical intervention and appropriate treatment significantly improve the chances of a full recovery.
